Lessons.Title: Division Situation Drawings
ExplanationParagraphs: The original 2021 Division Situation Drawings lesson compares two types of division story: in one the SIZE OF EACH GROUP is known and the NUMBER OF GROUPS is unknown; in another the NUMBER OF GROUPS is given and the NUMBER IN EACH is unknown. A completed equal-groups drawing can represent either interpretation if the quantities align.

Warm-up — Number Talk (10 minutes). Evaluate original 120+120,121+119,125+115 and129+111. ALL four expressions equal240. When one addend increases by the same amount that the other decreases, the sum stays constant. Explain this pattern without four isolated calculations.

Activity1 — Groups of Students (10 minutes). Distinguish 'groups OF 2' and '2 GROUPS'. Twelve children might be arranged in 6 groups of2 or in2 groups of6, but these arrangements mean different unknowns and are not interchangeable as drawings of a specifically given problem.

Activity2 — Elena's Colored Pencils (10 minutes). Elena has12 colored pencils, TWO boxes, equally shared. Each box gets 12÷2=6. The original teacher commentary explicitly identifies drawing A as TWO groups of SIX and drawing B as SIX groups of TWO. A matches Elena's situation; B does NOT match the known TWO boxes. First-party dot models show the same mathematics but are not the original illustration pixels.

Activity3 — Which Drawing Matches? (15 minutes). Figure A is described as TWO groups of FOUR dots: it represents Mai's 8 markers packed4 per box (unknown2 boxes) and Lin's 8 pencils equally shared into2 bags (unknown4 in each bag). In the first story, count groups; in the second, count dots per group.

Figure B is TEN groups of TWO dots: Kiran has20 pens and2 pens per table (unknown10 tables), while Noah shares20 pencils into10 boxes (unknown2 per box). Figure C is THREE groups of FIVE dots: Priya distributes15 crayons with5 per desk (unknown3 desks), while Jada distributes15 markers into3 tables equally (unknown5 per table). Each source drawing matches TWO stories because the final completed grouping is compatible with either question.

Use clear units and explain which factor is the unknown. Independent Edulytics drawings are source-mathematics-aligned, not copies of eight publisher image assets. Teacher validates diagrams, classroom conversation and source letter context; the original Party Favors Cool-down remains gated and not reproduced. Tests and Stage D have not run.

KeyConcepts.Title: Number of groups unknown
KeyConcepts.Definition: The total and the number of objects per group are known.
KeyConcepts.Rule: number of groups = total ÷ objects per group

KeyConcepts.Title: Group size unknown
KeyConcepts.Definition: The total and the number of groups are known.
KeyConcepts.Rule: objects per group = total ÷ number of groups
KeyConcepts.Example: Lin 8 colored pencils,2 bags →4 pencils per bag.

KeyConcepts.Title: One drawing, two problems
KeyConcepts.Definition: An array showing fixed groups can model either a group-count or group-size question.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Identify the unknown from the story words, NOT the picture alone.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two groups of four represents both Mai and Lin.

KeyConcepts.Title: Constant sum
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equal increase in one addend and decrease in the other leaves their sum unchanged.

WorkedExamples.Title: Elena's two boxes
WorkedExamples.Question: 12 pencils shared into 2 boxes equally. Which representation?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use number of groups GIVEN by the story.
Steps: Diagram A in the original teacher narrative has2 groups of6.
Diagram B has6 groups of2, hence doesn't represent two boxes.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 6 pencils each; source Elena figure A.

WorkedExamples.Title: Mai and Lin on one diagram
WorkedExamples.Question: How can two groups of4 model two different stories?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the group diagram based on which quantity is asked.
Steps: Mai:8 markers,4 per box; therefore2 boxes.
Lin:8 pencils,2 bags; therefore4 each bag.
Both finish with two equal groups of four.

WorkedExamples.Title: Figure B pairs
WorkedExamples.Question: Kiran gives2 pens per table from20; Noah fills10 boxes from20. What are unknowns?
Steps: Each finished picture has10 groups with2 objects each.

WorkedExamples.Title: Figure C pairs
WorkedExamples.Question: Priya has15 crayons at5 per desk; Jada has15 markers into3 tables.
Steps: The completed representation has3 groups of5.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume Elena's six groups of two is equivalent to two boxes.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Even though both diagrams total12, the number of boxes specified by the original story is2.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose two groups of six, labeled source A.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Say a dot drawing must represent only one verbal division problem.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The same finished groups can be described with different known and unknown quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Relate both stories to each group layout and label the unknown.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: For Noah respond ten pencils per box.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Ten is the GIVEN number of boxes; the task asks pencils each.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume original lettered drawings are exact publisher pixel copies.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Only mathematical group sizes and teacher descriptions are checked.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label independently authored dots and keep publisher visual parity unverified.

SummaryPoints: Elena 12÷2=6 each: original source A=two groups of six, not B=six groups of two.
Activity3 A(two×four) links Mai2 boxes and Lin4 each.
Activity3 B(ten×two) links Kiran10 tables and Noah2 each.
Activity3 C(three×five) links Priya3 desks and Jada5 each.
Math mapping is source-grounded; publisher image pixels, gated Cool-down and Stage D remain outside verified scope.
